title: Der Rosenkavalier
facts: Der Rosenkavalier premiered in Dresden on 26 January 1911 and was a triumph from the start; tickets reportedly sold out almost immediately.
Until the premiere the working title was “Ochs auf Lerchenau”. “Ochs” means “ox”, which describes the Baron’s manners.
Strauss filled the score with Viennese waltzes, an anachronism: the story is set in the 1740s, before the waltz was famous in Vienna.
Some critics objected to the anachronistic waltzes, but the public embraced the opera unconditionally.
Alfred Roller designed the original sets and costumes, and Strauss and Hofmannsthal had his designs published in a prompt book that all productions had to use.
Max Reinhardt was quietly brought in to help with rehearsals as a “shadow director”, though Georg Toller remained the only credited director.
The opera showcases the female voice: Sophie, Octavian and the Marschallin are all sung by women, who share a trio at the opera’s emotional climax.
Some singers have performed two or even all three of the leading female roles over their careers.
The Met gave the opera’s US premiere on 9 December 1913, conducted by Alfred Hertz.
Within two months of its premiere it was translated into Italian and performed at La Scala.
In the Marschallin’s reverie on the passing of time, a clock is heard chiming 13 times.
Strauss and Hofmannsthal mark social class through language: Octavian’s “Mariandl” and other non-noble characters speak an Austrian dialect.
